newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gas firms seek strategic edge in deregulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gas firms seek strategic edge in deregulation.

text.p: Faced with more competition as services are unbundled beyond the city gate, U.S. natural gas firms are looking for ways to cut costs and develop new strategies to survive in a newly-deregulated industry.
Since 1993 when federal laws forced pipelines to unbundle, the industry has gone through massive changes, including a wave of mergers and alliances, in the search for a strategic edge.
"Driven by anticipation of more deregulation, people are looking for a competitive advantage," Duane Windsor, professor at Rice University, told a gas conference here.
And while "merger mania" shows no signs of slowing, the focus now is on deregulation at the burner tip, which has triggered a scramble to find new roads to retail customers.

"I think many of the mergers we have seen are driven less by the need to be big than by the need for companies to achieve a critical mass of retail customers," said Catherine Good Abbott, CEO of Columbia Gas Transmission Corp.
States like New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Georgia have implemented pilot programs that allow even homeowners to choose their supplier, and more plans are on the way.
"By the turn of the century, almost everyone in America will have choice. This is going to play havoc with the way we operate," said Equitable Resources Inc CEO Frederick Abrew.

Rice's Windsor said the industry was in a transition phase, where firms were looking for position and thinking about either merging with or eliminating competitors. But he said there were opportunities for all kinds of players.
"All changes in market conditions and industry structure create new winners and losers. There are opportunities to be profitable, but there are also opportunities to go bankrupt."

Richard McCullough, executive vice president at the Municipal Gas Authority of Georgia (MGAG), agreed the recent wave of industry consolidations needed to be closely monitored to understand how competiton and markets were evolving.
"We better be looking ahead and adapting to change. We will continue to look for regional alliances and alliances with other agencies, either gas or electric," McCullough said.

MGAG, a non-profit state agency that provides gas supply and services to municipal systems, recently formed Public Energy Partners with Virginia Power to help it stay abreast of developments on the electric side of deregulation.
And while some thought only size mattered in a competitive marketplace, others saw a place for smaller firms that can react to change quickly.

"The small guy can identify his role and key in on specific areas of opportunity. He's better adapted to quick changes," said Keith Maxwell at Wickford Energy Marketing, a small Texas- based aggregator.
Maxwell said the key to survival of the small marketer was keeping costs low, building a loyal customer base and remaining flexible to changing market conditions.
"Success for the small aggregator is tied to servicing customer needs better than a large company can and more efficiently," he said.
